rationale: B wins because it found the sharpest skeptical story in the fact block: "Airtable just gave AI agents write access to enterprise data. What happens when one gets it wrong?" That turns missing reliability data into an editorial gate, not a footnote. A is solid, but "Airtable just entered the AI agent market — that changes who it competes with" is the more generic version: competitive fog until somebody names the competitors. B is more useful because it tells the founder what to pitch and what to hold.
gaps_in_A: "The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market" spends proof it does not yet have. One Airtable announcement is not a market turn unless you can show parallel moves.

"Airtable just entered the AI agent market — that changes who it competes with" is too broad. Without named competitor classes or buyer comparisons, this is a standard enterprise-software collision story in a nicer coat.
"all-in product pivot" overstates the supplied facts. We know Airtable is repositioning and launching agents; we do not know this is an all-in pivot or the path to closing a valuation gap.
It notices "Is Airtable willing to share any reliability or error-rate data" but leaves it as homework. That should have been a kept governance angle, not just an uncomfortable question.
gaps_in_B: "pre-AI decacorns rebrand to survive" imports a broader press narrative the fact block did not supply. Valuation pressure is real; death-watch framing is not.
"formally retiring the \"spreadsheet-database\" identity it was built on" is too absolute. The update says Airtable is shifting messaging, not killing the old identity.

"angles one and two are pitchable from the facts on file" is a little generous. Angle two still needs a demo, permission model, pricing direction, or customer before it becomes more than launch-news calories.
